name: Shooter
description: Weapons, movement and AI in levels built for firefights, with an optional Networking doc for multiplayer.

pillars.name: Gunplay First
pillars.feeling: every shot feels punchy and precise

pillars.name: Readable Fights
pillars.feeling: I always know where the threat is
pillars.rulesOut: visual noise, silent or unseen attackers

pillars.name: Enemies Worth Outsmarting
pillars.feeling: the AI fights back and I outplay it
pillars.rulesOut: bullet sponges, enemies that stand still

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A fast first-person shooter where squads of smart enemies make every firefight a puzzle of cover and timing.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Spawn with a loadout.
2. Push through an encounter.
3. Outplay the AI with movement and weapons.
4. Resupply and push to the next objective.

docs.title: Weapons
docs.summary: How guns feel and differ.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can carry two weapons and switch quickly.
- As a player, I can feel the difference between weapon types.
- As a player, I can pick up weapons from the world.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Ammo count and weapon name on the HUD.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Switching takes under half a second.
- Each weapon type has a clear role (close, mid, long range).

docs.title: Recoil and Spread
docs.summary: Recoil patterns, spread and how they reward control.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can control recoil with practice.
- As a player, I can fire accurately while still.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - The crosshair grows with spread.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Recoil follows a learnable pattern.
- Moving increases spread; crouching reduces it.

docs.title: Ammo and Reloading
docs.summary: Magazines, reserves, reloads and pickups.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can reload when I choose.
- As a player, I can see how much ammo is left.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A low-ammo warning on the HUD.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Reloading with a round chambered is faster.
- Ammo pickups are shared across weapons of a type.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.summary: Scopes, grips and other modifiers, and how they change a weapon.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can add scopes, grips and magazines to weapons.
- As a player, I can see how an attachment changes a weapon.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Stat bars that change as I preview attachments.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Each weapon has up to four attachment slots.
- Every attachment has a trade-off.

docs.title: Weapon System
docs.summary: Hitscan or projectiles, fire rates, hit detection and weapon data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Weapons are actors with a firing component. Hitscan weapons trace on the server and clients; projectile weapons spawn predicted projectiles. Weapon stats come from data assets.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `AWeaponBase`: firing, reloading and attachments
- `UWeaponData`: data asset with fire rate, damage, recoil pattern
- `UHitscanComponent`: traces and hit confirmation

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Weapon stats and recoil curves in UWeaponData.
- Attachment modifiers in a DataTable.

docs.summary: Weapon meshes, first-person animations, muzzle flashes and gun sounds.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Grounded near-future: believable weapons with clean shapes and some wear.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Weapon packs with first-person rigs and animations.
- Gun sound libraries with close, distant and indoor variations.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Fantasy or cartoon weapons.
- Weapons without separate magazine bones.

docs.title: Player Movement
docs.summary: Running, crouching, sliding, mantling and how movement interacts with aiming.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can sprint, crouch, slide and mantle.
- As a player, I can keep aiming while moving.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Camera bob and sway that stay subtle.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Sliding is triggered by crouching while sprinting.
- Mantling works on ledges up to chest height.

docs.title: Movement Code
docs.summary: The movement component, mantling traces and tuning values.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A custom character movement component adds slide and mantle modes. Mantles use forward and down traces to find a ledge.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UShooterMovementComponent`: slide and mantle modes
- `UMantleComponent`: ledge traces and mantle animation

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Speeds and slide friction in a data asset.
- Mantle heights and trace distances.

docs.summary: First- and third-person animation sets.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Weighty but responsive: animations never delay input.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- First-person arm rigs with weapon animation sets.
- Third-person locomotion packs with crouch and slide.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Long animations that lock out input.

docs.title: AI
docs.summary: Enemies that fight back believably.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can fight enemies that use cover and flank.
- As a player, I can outsmart enemies with positioning.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Enemies call out what they're doing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Enemies never shoot through walls.
- Enemies react to sound.

docs.title: Cover
docs.summary: Finding, using and leaving cover.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can see enemies take and leave cover.
- As a player, I can flush enemies out of cover with grenades.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Enemies peeking from cover.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Enemies leave cover when flanked.
- Destructible cover breaks after enough damage.

docs.title: Squad Behavior
docs.summary: How AI coordinates: flanking, suppression and callouts.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can face squads that coordinate.
- As a player, I can break a squad's plan by taking out its leader.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Audible callouts when enemies flank or reload.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Squads have one leader.
- No more than two enemies flank at once.

docs.title: Perception
docs.summary: What AI can see and hear, and how it notices the player.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: AI perception gives enemies sight and hearing. Stimuli feed a threat score per target that decides who they attack.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UAIPerceptionComponent`: sight and hearing senses
- `UThreatComponent`: keeps threat scores per target

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Sight cone and range per enemy type.
- Hearing ranges per sound event.

docs.title: AI Framework
docs.summary: Behavior trees, EQS queries and how squads share information.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Enemies run behavior trees; EQS queries find cover and flanking spots. A squad manager hands out roles so enemies don't all do the same thing.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `AEnemyController`: runs the behavior tree
- `USquadSubsystem`: squad roles and shared target info
- `EQS_FindCover`: query for cover spots

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Behavior trees per enemy type.
- Squad roles in a data asset.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Each enemy type has a distinct silhouette and color so the player recognizes it instantly.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Creature packs with idle, move, attack, hit and death animations.
- Packs with several variants on one skeleton.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Enemies that look like the player or allies.
- Animation sets missing hit or death animations.

docs.title: Levels
docs.summary: Maps built for firefights: sightlines, cover placement and flow.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can move through each level and always know where to go next.
- As a player, I can find side paths that reward curiosity.
- As a player, I can see where I've been and where I haven't.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Landmarks visible from far away.
- Light and color that guide me toward the main path.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every level has a clear start, goal and one optional reward.
- Levels teach a new idea before testing it.

- Cover prop packs with collision.

examples.heading: What to Avoid

docs.title: Game Modes
docs.summary: The rules of each mode: objectives, scoring and rounds.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can pick a mode from a menu.
- As a player, I can understand each mode's goal before starting.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Mode rules on the loading screen.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Each mode has a time limit.
- Modes share the same weapons.

docs.title: Networking
docs.summary: Multiplayer: replication, lag compensation and matchmaking. Remove if single-player.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The server is authoritative; clients predict their own movement and the server corrects them. Only what the client needs is replicated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `Replicated properties and RPCs`: on gameplay actors
- `UNetworkSettings`: tick rates and relevancy distances

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Net update frequencies per actor class.
- Bandwidth budget per player.

docs.title: Replication
docs.summary: What's synced, how often, and who has authority.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Actors replicate state with replicated properties and events with RPCs. Relevancy keeps far-away actors from being sent.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `GetLifetimeReplicatedProps`: declares replicated state per actor
- `Server RPCs`: client requests the server validates

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Net update frequency and priority per actor class.
- Which properties replicate to owner only.

docs.title: Matchmaking
docs.summary: Finding, joining and balancing matches.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Players create or join sessions through the online subsystem. A host advertises a session; others search and join it. Parties travel together.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USessionSubsystem`: creates, finds and joins sessions
- `UPartyComponent`: keeps friends together when joining

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Session settings (max players, map, mode).
- Platform online subsystem config.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|

| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: HUD
docs.summary: Crosshair, ammo, health, hit markers and the scoreboard.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can see health, ammo and objectives at a glance.
- As a player, I can see where damage came from.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Hit markers and damage direction indicators.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- The HUD can be scaled.
- Nothing important sits in the screen's center except the crosshair.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.
